function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that you’ll need to add to the repo.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to the remote repository from here, but the commands below will do it for you on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH access, use the HTTPS URL instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a simple Node.js/Express app (`app.js`) that listens on port **3000**.  
Create a `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Use the official lightweight Node.js image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first (for caching)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small and fast.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the app’s listening port.  
> * `CMD ["node", "app.js"]` is the default entrypoint.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can create a `k8s` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your image registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app on port 80 inside the cluster (targeting container port 3000).  
> * Uses `ClusterIP` – change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Docker Buildx
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (replace with your own registry if needed)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the Docker image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

      # (Optional) Deploy to a Kubernetes cluster
      # Uncomment and configure the following if you have a kubeconfig secret
      # - name: Deploy to K8s
      #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
      #   with:
      #     manifests: k8s/deployment.yaml
      #     kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the Docker image and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> * You can extend it to deploy to a cluster if you store a kubeconfig in a secret.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repo
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run and build your Docker image.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .

# Run the container locally
docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:local
```

If you see the app running on `http://localhost:3000`, everything is wired correctly.

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image |

Feel free to tweak the image registry, tags, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. Happy coding!
